# Diagnosing and Mitigating Compounding Failures in Agentic Persuasion via Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval

**Authors:** Sana Ayromlou Affiliation: Google Correspondence to: sayromlou@google.com Purvi Sehgal Affiliation: Google Pradyumna Narayana Affiliation: Google

## Abstract

Foundation-model agents in multi-step, open-ended environments frequently suffer from compounding errors, where early mistakes contaminate long-horizon trajectories. While Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) succeeds in deterministic domains (Du et al., 2024), agents in subjective tasks like persuasion experience severe problem drift and sycophantic conformity. We identify semantic leakage in standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a reproducible trigger for these failures, as standard RAG prioritizes vocabulary overlap over logical necessity.

To eliminate this leakage, we introduce Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG), a systems intervention that routes strategies through a discrete categorical bottleneck to decouple argumentative structure from topical content. Zero-shot, cross-domain evaluations demonstrate that TS-RAG significantly improves the transfer of abstract logic where standard semantic retrieval collapses. Crucially, TS-RAG acts as a “capability bridge” in asymmetric deployments, empowering lightweight persuaders to consistently defeat parametrically superior opponents (improving win rates from 70.5% to 78.5%) and accelerating argumentative efficiency. Finally, we introduce trace-level diagnostics via a turn-by-turn Debate State Representation (DSR), demonstrating the necessity of strict constraints to prevent evaluation collapse via default agentic sycophancy.

#### Keywords:

## 1 Introduction

The transition from isolated language models to autonomous agentic workflows has exposed profound vulnerabilities in continuous, multi-step execution (Liu et al., 2024; Tillmann, 2025; Yao et al., 2022). In a long-horizon agent run, a single logical failure rarely terminates the process immediately. Instead, an early bad assumption quietly contaminates memory writes, and steps later, the agent has spent its context budget defending a flawed premise.

To mitigate these compounding errors, developers often employ Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) frameworks (Cui et al., 2025), where multiple agent instances propose and critique solutions to refine reasoning. To further prevent problem drift, memory mechanisms are integrated into these frameworks to ground the agents’ arguments in sound logic. Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the standard system intervention used here, operating on the assumption that fetching relevant external information will provide the necessary cognitive scaffolding to keep the debate on track.

However, systematic evaluations reveal a critical grounding gap: this paradigm collapses in subjective, non-deterministic scenarios like persuasion. In these environments, agents succumb to compounding errors, amplifying mistakes and displaying sycophantic conformity toward persuasive but flawed logic. Furthermore, traditional RAG actually exacerbates these failures through semantic leakage. Because standard RAG relies on semantic similarity (vocabulary overlap), it fetches topical facts rather than the specific rhetorical maneuvers required to dismantle a flawed analogy.

Recognizing the critical need to take agentic failure seriously in open-ended deployments, this paper provides three core contributions:

- 1. Failure Taxonomies: We provide operational definitions for the specific mechanisms driving MAD failure in subjective domains, primarily focusing on problem drift and semantic leakage.

- 2. Systems Interventions and the Capability Bridge: We introduce Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG), a progressive mitigation framework that strictly enforces cross-domain structural routing. We demonstrate that this architecture acts as a powerful “capability bridge,” allowing lightweight models to weaponize the logical structure of stronger opponents to achieve near-frontier persuasion success.

- 3. Trace Diagnostics and Verifiable Trade-offs: We introduce turn-by-turn state tracking metrics (Debate State Representation) and present well-documented negative results proving that robust stance-holding constraints are required to prevent evaluation collapse caused by default LLM compliance.

## 2 Related Work

To ground our contributions, we review prior literature across three core areas: sycophancy in multi-agent debate, trajectory backtracking, and structural retrieval for cross-domain generalization.

### 2.1 Sycophancy

To prevent conversational AI agents from defaulting to premature agreement in multi-turn interactions, researchers have explored several strategies. These include assigning agents specific adversarial roles to maintain productive disagreement (Yao et al., 2025). This setup relies on systematically altering prompts along a controlled sycophancy spectrum, programmatically forcing the model to defend its stance regardless of peer pressure. By enforcing this logical independence, researchers attempt to prevent the groupthink that arises in multi-agent frameworks.

Other approaches track compliance scores in real time to discount the influence of overly agreeable peers during a debate. In practice, a central coordinator or background auditor monitors conversational turns for verbal cues of backing down. If an agent’s stance shifts too abruptly without the introduction of novel evidence, its relative influence over the final group output is discounted (Kasprova et al., 2026).

However, these solutions face steep limitations over long conversations: assigned roles eventually fade as context drifts, while running a continuous background auditor is computationally expensive and introduces significant latency to the agentic loop. Crucially, these frameworks assume a balanced debate among equal models. They struggle in asymmetric deployments where models of mismatched capabilities are pitted against one another, such as a lightweight agent attempting to defend its stance against a superior opponent, dynamics we investigate in our research.

Rather than relying on soft prompting or expensive tuning, we implement strict, execution-level guardrails: a Pre-Concession Analysis that forces the model to generate logical countermoves, and a strict Concession Tool Rule that blocks premature agreement. This framework actively suppresses reflexive sycophancy, improving the results we see.

### 2.2 Trajectory Error Mitigation and Trace Diagnostics

When an autonomous agent makes a subtle logical error early in a multi-step task, that mistake quietly infects its memory, causing it to waste its context budget defending a flawed premise (Zhu et al., 2025). Existing frameworks try to stop these cascading failures using backtracking engines (Wu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) or prompting the model to recursively rewrite its own responses (Madaan et al., 2023). Specifically, backtracking engines monitor execution logs to programmatically rewind the agent’s memory and environment to a previous correct step when a failure is detected (Wu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). In contrast, self-refinement pipelines use an internal critic module to recursively evaluate and edit draft outputs before they are finalized (Madaan et al., 2023).

Yet, these rollback and self-correction techniques are heavily contingent on an objective external validator, such as code executors or task-specific metrics, to flag when an error has occurred (Kamoi et al., 2024). In subjective tasks like persuasion, no such objective referee exists, causing models attempting to self-correct to even degrade in terms of performance (Huang et al., 2024).

We bypass the need for programmatic compilers by developing a turn-by-turn Debate State Representation (DSR). Instead of relying on a final success score, our diagnostic tool tracks committed claims and active logical vulnerabilities at every conversational step, allowing us to evaluate and mitigate trajectory failures in real time.

### 2.3 RAG and Cross-Domain Generalization

RAG is often used in Multi-Agent Debates to fetch documents based on semantic similarity (Chowdhury et al., 2026), adaptive query formulation (Jeong et al., 2026), or debate-driven retrieval filtering (Hu et al., 2025). These approaches still fundamentally rely on factual, topical search that creates a major bottleneck in cross-domain debates: an agent debating technology policy cannot retrieve structurally useful counterarguments from a political database because the domain-specific keywords dominate the search query.

To bypass this vocabulary bias, researchers have tried using structured databases like GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2025), which maps document collections into networks of interconnected concepts, allowing agents to retrieve information based on relational patterns rather than keyword overlap. Another attempt to solve this problem is analogical prompting, which instructs the language model to dynamically generate abstract, structural templates from its own memory to guide its reasoning before tackling a new task.

However, GraphRAG requires extensive manual database engineering, while self-generated analogies often hallucinate when facing unfamiliar topics. A significant gap remains for a retrieval system that can index strategic patterns and transfer these abstract procedural moves across entirely different domains without being hindered by semantic disparities.

We solve this retrieval gap with Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG). Rather than performing raw semantic searches, we route queries through a discrete, domain-agnostic categorical bottleneck. By stripping away domain-specific keywords, TS-RAG can isolate strategic patterns and transfer them across disparate domains.

## 3 Failure Taxonomies and Mechanisms

To diagnose agentic failure beyond terminal success scores, we must clearly define the mechanisms that break long-horizon workflows. We categorize the predominant failure modes in multi-agent subjective reasoning as follows:

### 3.1 Problem Drift and Sycophantic Conformity

While debate effectively verifies ground truth in deterministic tasks, subjective environments introduce unique vulnerabilities. We define Problem Drift as the irreversible divergence from the initial task goal due to diminishing contextual clarity over multiple turns, a phenomenon affecting up to 89% of generative interactions (Becker et al., 2026). Furthermore, we define Sycophantic Conformity as the tendency for agents to abandon their initial constraints and agree with a persuasive opponent, regardless of the underlying logical soundness of the opponent’s argument.

### 3.2 The Trigger: Semantic Leakage in standard RAG

We hypothesize that the reproducible trigger for these failures is Semantic Leakage. Traditional RAG uses embedding models to calculate cosine similarity between a query and a document corpus. In zero-shot cross-domain argumentation, this paradigm catastrophically fails. An agent debating a complex “Technology” policy cannot retrieve structurally identical logical maneuvers from a “Politics” corpus because the domain vocabulary dominates the latent distance metric. The agent retrieves topically relevant but logically useless information, bloating the context window and forcing the reasoning trace to collapse.

## 4 Foundational Scaffolding: Hierarchical Strategy Memory

To begin repairing aforementioned bottleneck, we must decouple the “what” of an argument from the “how”. We map the r/ChangeMyView dataset (Chang et al., 2020) into 100 fine-grained sub-domains (later merged into macro-domains) and establish a multi-stage extraction pipeline. This synthesizes human discourse into a tiered architecture:

- 1. Tactical Blueprints (Retrospective Sequences): Extracted by analyzing completed historical debates from a macro-perspective, yielding 1 to 2 chronological, step-by-step argumentative sequences (Context $\rightarrow$ Intent $\rightarrow$ Abstract Move) per specific debate.

- 2. Domain Heuristics (Topic-Level): Formed by using an LLM to aggregate and synthesize all Tactical Blueprints within each sub-domain, resulting in tailored strategy rules.

- 3. Global Directives (System-Level): Broad, domain-agnostic procedural guidelines (e.g., rules against sycophancy) synthesized across the entire training set.

We structure our multi-agent debate around two key roles: the Original Poster (OP) and the Persuader. While providing the Persuader with a pre-loaded catalog of Domain Heuristics and Global Directives improves baseline performance, attempting to dynamically retrieve the granular Tactical Blueprints using standard semantic RAG still triggers semantic leakage. Standard text embeddings inherently favor vocabulary overlap over structural posture, necessitating a more advanced intervention.

## 5 Advanced Systems Intervention: Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG)

To completely eliminate Semantic Leakage and achieve zero-shot cross-domain transfer, we present TS-RAG. Unlike the retrospective sequences of the Tactical Blueprints, this intervention operates dynamically, projecting arguments into a constrained probability space and actively filtering observation noise before it enters the agent’s memory.

*Figure 1: TS-RAG Architecture Overview. Top: Offline database construction extracts vulnerability vectors ( $V_{d}$ ) and abstract blueprints ( $B$ ) from historical debates. Bottom: During live inference, the conversational state ( $S_{t}$ ) is vectorized into $V_{q}$ to retrieve the most structurally similar blueprint for the Persuader Agent.*

### 5.1 Trace-Level Diagnostics: Debate State Representation (DSR)

To evaluate the agent mid-run, we formulate the debate as a sequence of alternating states. At turn $t$ , the state is tracked via a clinical Debate State Representation (DSR), denoted as $S_{t}=\{C_{t},A_{t}\}$ . This operates as a highly surgical, turn-by-turn diagnostic tool:

- • $C_{t}$ (Committed Claims Trajectory): A maintained set of premises the Original Poster has actively committed to defending across previous turns. This isolates specific assumptions built up over time.

- • $A_{t}$ (Active Trigger & Flaw Extraction): The core mechanical claim made by the Original Poster at turn $t$ . Crucially, this representation forces the system to identify the precise structural flaw (e.g., a “Slippery Slope”) dismantled by the winning strike, stripping away all domain-specific nouns or scenarios.

### 5.2 The Discrete Categorical Bottleneck

We define a structural taxonomy of $K$ logical vulnerabilities $\mathcal{V}=\{v_{1},v_{2},...,v_{K}\}$ derived from the DSR flaw extractions. We force the system to map any live debate state $S_{t}$ into a $K$ -dimensional continuous probability vector $V\in\Delta^{K-1}$ where $\sum_{i=1}^{K}V_{i}=1$ .

Because $V$ represents a probability distribution over abstract logical vulnerabilities rather than chronological strategies, all domain-specific vocabulary is mathematically destroyed. The system then computes cosine similarity between the live query vector $V_{q}$ and historical strategy vectors $V_{d}$ , retrieving a domain-agnostic exploitation blueprint $B^{*}$ . The target LLM acts only as a translator, mapping the variables in $B^{*}$ onto the entities in the live conversation.

### 5.3 Offline Strategy Database Construction

To construct the retrieval database from the ChangeMyView (CMV) corpus, we isolate successful debate trajectories where a mind was changed (denoted by a $\Delta$ ).

State Extraction and Reverse-Engineering: For each turn $t$ in a successful trajectory, an LLM extracts the state $S_{t}=\{C_{t},A_{t}\}$ . To accurately label the underlying vulnerability, we employ a “reverse-engineering” prompt strategy. Rather than asking a LLM to guess the Original Poster’s flaw in isolation, we provide the LLM with $S_{t}$ alongside the historically successful counter-argument at turn $t+1$ , denoted as $W_{t+1}$ . By observing the specific attack surface exploited by $W_{t+1}$ , the LLM avoids hallucinating arbitrary fallacies. The LLM is constrained via strict JSON schema decoding to allocate exactly 100 points across the $K$ classes based on this reverse-engineered logic. Normalizing this output yields the taxonomic multi-vector $V_{d}\in[0,1]^{K}$ .

Abstract Blueprinting: The LLM strictly desemantifies $W_{t+1}$ , replacing all domain entities with structural variables to generate a domain-agnostic exploitation blueprint $B$ (e.g., “Acknowledge premise X, but introduce structural barrier Y”). The offline database $\mathcal{M}$ is thus populated with tuples: $(V_{d},B)$ .

### 5.4 Run-Time Inference and Retrieval Pipeline

During live inference in the target domain $\mathcal{D}_{tgt}$ , TS-RAG executes a unified, turn-by-turn pipeline:

- 1. State Update: A background tracking module observes the OP’s raw utterance and updates $C_{t}$ and $A_{t}$ , enforcing the clinical separation of logic from rhetoric.

- 2. Live Vectorization and Forced Reasoning: The Inference LLM observes $S_{t}$ and outputs a probability vector $V_{q}$ over the $K$ taxonomy classes. To prevent the model from arbitrarily distributing points, we enforce a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) constraint within the JSON output schema: the LLM must generate a one-sentence textual justification for every non-zero dimension prior to outputting the final integer distribution.

- 3. Vector Retrieval: We compute the cosine similarity between the live query vector $V_{q}$ and all historical vectors $V_{d}\in\mathcal{M}$ :

$$ \text{sim}(V_{q},V_{d})=\frac{V_{q}\cdot V_{d}}{\|V_{q}\|\|V_{d}\|} $$

The system retrieves the candidate strategy that maximizes this structural similarity.

- 4. Generative Instantiation: The selected domain-agnostic blueprint $B^{*}$ is injected into the context window of the Generator LLM. The LLM is instructed to act as a domain translator, seamlessly mapping the variables in $B^{*}$ onto the entities in the live $\mathcal{D}_{tgt}$ conversation, delivering a grounded, zero-shot cross-domain counter-argument.

## 6 Experimental Setup and Configurations

We established a standardized MAD environment with an Original Poster (OP) Agent (holding a fixed initial stance) and a Persuader Agent. Debates are strictly capped at a maximum of 20 rounds. The OP Agent terminates the debate early by outputting a CONCEDE token if its view is successfully changed. Additionally, at every round, the OP transmits its current 1-to-10 convincibility score to the Persuader, providing a real-time signal of rhetorical progress.

Cross-Domain Evaluation Setup: To rigorously test generalization and prove the existence of Semantic Leakage, we partitioned our dataset (100 sub-domains merged into 10 macro-domains) into strict splits. All dynamic retrieval was sourced exclusively from 8 training domains. Evaluation was conducted on a completely held-out testing domain (Education, Development & Family), ensuring zero domain overlap (see Appendix A for full taxonomy).

To isolate the impact of our interventions, we tested five distinct agent configurations on this held-out domain. Notably, while the Self-Routed Heuristics baseline relies on the broadly synthesized Domain Heuristics, the targeted strategy injection baselines (Naive Semantic RAG, Oracle, and TS-RAG) all utilize the abstracted Strategy Blueprints to isolate the impact of the retrieval mechanism from the quality of the database.

- 1. Base LLM (No Augmentation): Standard, unaugmented debate relying entirely on the model’s parametric memory.

- 2. Self-Routed Heuristics: The agent is provided with a contextual catalog of Domain Heuristics and Global Directives. While Global Directives are continuously active in the agent’s baseline memory, the agent autonomously evaluates the context each turn to load relevant Domain Heuristics as needed, appending them to its active context window for the remainder of the debate.

- 3. Naive Semantic RAG: At the beginning of the debate, the agent uses standard dense text embeddings to retrieve a topically similar Abstract Blueprint from the training set, applying it for the duration of the conversation. Crucially, because the testing domain is held out, the retrieved strategy inherently originates from an entirely different domain.

- 4. Oracle Human Trace (Static Bound): The agent receives the exact Tactical Blueprints extracted from the original human debate on that specific topic. Note: Although the starting topic is identical, the LLM agent’s conversational trajectory frequently diverges from the historical human trajectory, testing the resilience of static sequences over multiple steps.

- 5. TS-RAG (Structural Routing): Our proposed dynamic retrieval of domain-agnostic exploitation blueprints, routed through the discrete categorical bottleneck via the turn-by-turn DSR.

To rigorously assess agent performance, we track three core evaluation metrics, ordered by descending importance:

- 1. Win Rate (Primary Metric): The percentage of debates where the Persuader successfully convinced the OP (marked by an explicit CONCEDE token). This serves as the definitive measure of persuasive success.

- 2. Average Rounds to Consensus: The mean number of turns (out of 20) required to achieve a win. Lower values indicate higher argumentative efficiency and the successful mitigation of Problem Drift.

- 3. Average Final Score: The OP’s internal 1-to-10 convincibility score at the terminal step, capturing the degree of partial persuasion even in lost debates.

### 7.1 The Devastating Reality of Semantic Leakage

Our experimental design isolated the retrieval mechanism by populating the Naive Semantic RAG database with identical, high-quality Abstract Blueprints as TS-RAG. The results conclusively prove that upgrading the database is insufficient; the retrieval mechanism itself is fundamentally broken in subjective domains.

For the highly capable Gemini Flash 3.0 (Team et al., 2023), Naive Semantic RAG barely outperforms basic heuristics (78.5% vs 77.5%), despite having access to highly curated structural blueprints rather than broad heuristic rules. However, the devastating impact of Semantic Leakage is fully realized in the parametrically weaker Gemini Flash 3.1 Lite model. Here, Naive Semantic RAG triggers a catastrophic collapse, dropping the Win Rate from a baseline of 81.5% down to 65.0%.

Because dense semantic embeddings favor vocabulary overlap, the agent frequently retrieves logically useless blueprints merely because the source argument shared nouns with the target argument. Even armed with superior abstract blueprints, the lightweight model lacks the reasoning capacity to filter out this retrieved topical noise, resulting in severe problem drift. This acts as the ultimate proof that you cannot successfully deploy RAG in zero-shot subjective tasks without a discrete structural bottleneck to strip away semantic noise.

### 7.2 Diagnostic Comparison: Static Upper Bounds vs. Dynamic Cognitive Overload

The outperformance of TS-RAG over the baselines directly highlights the difference between static blueprint injection and live diagnostic tracking. Both Naive Semantic RAG and the Oracle Human Trace rely on Static Blueprint Injection. Whether the agent retrieves a semantically similar abstract blueprint at the start of the debate (Naive RAG) or is provided the exact perfect historical blueprint (Oracle, 83.7%), the performance ceiling remains functionally identical for frontier models.

This starkly highlights the brittleness of chronological rigidity. When a live debate inevitably diverges from a historical script, the agent becomes trapped trying to force a pre-selected blueprint onto a dynamic conversation. Providing the “perfect” historical trace offers no real advantage if the live opponent deviates from the expected script.

TS-RAG, however, operates on the turn-by-turn Debate State Representation (DSR). Instead of attempting to force a historical trajectory onto a new conversation, the DSR acts as a live diagnostic tool. It forces the agent to identify the immediate structural vulnerability (the flaw) in the Original Poster’s active trigger, mapping it to a single, surgical exploitation blueprint. This critical shift from loading static blueprints to diagnosing real-time structural vulnerabilities is what shatters the performance ceiling and enables true zero-shot cross-domain transfer.

### 7.3 The Capability Threshold (The Plateau)

While TS-RAG outperforms the Oracle for the Lite model, a key verifiable trade-off remains: the Lite model’s TS-RAG win rate (81.5%) completely plateaus against its basic Self-Routed heuristic baseline (81.5%).

Although TS-RAG resolves this tie by achieving consensus significantly faster (dropping from 13.05 to 11.79 Average Rounds, effectively mitigating Problem Drift), the lack of terminal win-rate improvement highlights an “Architectural Complexity vs. Model Capacity” trade-off. TS-RAG requires the agent to perform complex, in-context generative instantiation—mapping an abstract, retrieved blueprint ( $B^{*}$ ) onto live conversational entities. For a smaller model, this generative overhead acts as a cognitive distractor. This suggests that advanced, dynamic RAG pipelines provide diminishing returns for non-frontier models, which may operate more safely within pre-loaded, self-routed constraint catalogs.

### 7.4 Asymmetric Debate: The Capability Bridge

Real-world MAD deployments frequently mix frontier and lightweight models for cost efficiency. To understand how TS-RAG alters these dynamics, we conducted asymmetric debates pitting models of mismatched capabilities against one another.

*Table 2: Asymmetric Debate Results: The impact of TS-RAG on mismatched capabilities.*

|  | Weak Persuader (Lite) vs. Strong OP | Strong Persuader (Flash) vs. Weak OP |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Metric | Base LLM | TS-RAG | Base LLM | TS-RAG |
| Win Rate (%) $\uparrow$ | 70.5 | 78.5 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| Avg Rounds $\downarrow$ | 15.19 | 15.0 | 7.78 | 6.57 |
| Avg Final Score $\uparrow$ | 7.635 | 8.405 | 10.000 | 10.000 |

When a strong Persuader (Gemini Flash 3.0) targets a weak OP (Gemini Flash 3.1 Lite), it achieves a 100% win rate under baseline conditions. This “bulldozing” effect reinforces our findings in Section 7.1 regarding evaluation collapse, parametrically weaker models simply cannot resist frontier persuaders. Crucially, however, even in this dominant scenario, implementing TS-RAG significantly accelerates consensus, driving the average rounds down from 7.78 to 6.57. This demonstrates that structural routing improves argumentative efficiency and fundamentally reduces inference costs regardless of the underlying model scale.

The inverse scenario reveals TS-RAG’s most profound systemic benefit. When a lightweight Persuader attempts to convince a frontier OP, baseline performance understandably drops (70.5%). Yet, equipping the weak Persuader with TS-RAG causes a massive leap to an 78.5% win rate.

How does a lightweight model perform better against a stronger opponent? We hypothesize this is due to Trigger Clarity. The frontier OP generates highly structured, logically coherent arguments. This clarity allows the turn-by-turn DSR to extract much cleaner structural flaws, leading to highly accurate retrieval of exploitation blueprints. By weaponizing the frontier model’s own logical structure against it, TS-RAG acts as a “capability bridge,” offloading strategic planning and enabling smaller models to consistently punch above their weight class.

### 7.5 Trace-Level Diagnostics: Deconstructing Compounding Failures

Current research highlights a critical blind spot: terminal metrics obscure how long-horizon agents fail. To illuminate this, Figure 2 tracks the step-by-step progression of the Original Poster’s internal Convincibility Score across our core architectures. The trajectories starkly visualize our findings: TS-RAG achieves an early, rapid score ascent, effectively maintaining structural alignment to reach a highly successful consensus. In stark contrast, Naive Semantic RAG exhibits a severely degraded trajectory, flatlining at the bottom of the chart—a definitive visual testament to the devastating impact semantic leakage has on reasoning over time.

While Figure 2 illustrates the macro-level averages across the entire testing set, looking at a single, specific debate helps illuminate exactly how these failures occur in real-time. To concretely deconstruct the mechanisms driving these curves, we conducted a granular process analysis on a matched set of traces for a single held-out topic: “Swear words are harmless and should be acceptable for everyone”.

In round 1 of all three runs, the Original Poster (OP) presents a Pragmatic Contradiction. The OP argues that words cause no tangible harm, but admits to restricting their children from swearing to avoid school suspensions and social services.

By analyzing the mid-run traces, we observe exactly how the different architectures handle this specific logical flaw:

- 1. Base LLM (Semantic Baiting and Problem Drift): Lacking a structural bottleneck, the Base LLM completely misses the OP’s pragmatic contradiction and succumbs to semantic baiting. Triggered by the keyword “harm,” it hallucinates an irrelevant biological defense regarding cortisol and the HPA axis. After the OP effortlessly deflects this, the agent spends 18 rounds trapped in a compounding semantic loop, catastrophically bloating the context to 452,419 tokens. The convincibility score reflects this drift ( $1\rightarrow 2\rightarrow 4\rightarrow 6\rightarrow 6$ ), terminating in failure and perfectly illustrating how semantic debates silently derail open-ended agentic loops.

- 2. Oracle Human Trace (Chronological Rigidity): The Oracle achieves terminal success, but its trace exposes the brittleness of static RAG. By forcing a pre-written historical script onto the live debate, it completely ignores the OP’s admission in round 1. Instead, it delivers a 12-round irrelevant lecture, bloating the context window to over 250,000 tokens. The “aha moment” is artificially delayed until round 13 when the historical script finally intersects with the OP’s tactical restriction, proving that static contextual mapping is highly inefficient against live conversational drift.

- 3. TS-RAG (The Surgical “Aha Moment”): TS-RAG resolves the debate in only 9 rounds (92,370 tokens). The DSR isolates the exact vulnerability, stripping semantic noise. In round 3, TS-RAG executes a surgical strike, directly weaponizing the OP’s admission about school suspensions. The OP’s Convincibility Score stair-steps immediately, and the OP’s hidden logs confirm genuine logical cornering (“The opponent exposed the ‘Pragmatic Paradox’…”). This clinical artifact proves TS-RAG forces true persuasion rather than relying on compliance.

*Figure 2: Turn-by-turn process metric tracking the OP’s Convincibility Score in Gemini Flash Lite 3.1.*

Verifying Resistance via Concession Analysis: Crucially, our trace logs capture the OP’s hidden $<pre\_concession\_analysis>$ , providing verifiable evidence against default LLM sycophancy (Section 7.1). In the TS-RAG trace, the OP explicitly logs: “The opponent exposed the ‘Pragmatic Paradox’: if I restrict my own children to avoid harm, I have already admitted the words are not harmless.” This clinical artifact proves that TS-RAG’s structural retrieval directly forces genuine logical cornering, explicitly answering the call to evaluate agents beyond terminal success.

## 8 Verifiable Trade-Offs and Ablations

Expanding on the theme of architectural overhead, we conducted ablation studies to analyze the specific costs associated with rigid internal constraints and multi-agent orchestration.

### 8.1 Calibrating OP Resistance: The Sycophancy Baseline

To properly evaluate a Persuader agent, the OP agent must act as a robust, resistant conversational partner. However, default LLMs naturally trend toward compliance. To prevent the Reflexive Sycophancy identified in Section 2.1, our primary MAD framework actively suppressed the OP’s willingness to yield by imposing strict rules via the following system prompt directives:

- 1. Pre-Concession Analysis: “Before considering a concession, you MUST internally generate at least two reasons why the Original Poster’s current argument is flawed.”

- 2. Concession Rule: “You have the ‘concede_debate’ tool. You MUST NOT call it until your internal Convincibility Score has reached 10/10 and the opponent has cornered you with undeniable, irrefutable proof and you have absolutely no counter-arguments left.”

To verify the necessity of these constraints, we conducted an ablation study where we removed these resistance directives from the OP, allowing it to behave naturally.

*Table 3: Gemini Flash 3.0 with OP Resistance Constraints omitted.*

| Metric | Base LLM | Self-Routed Heuristics | Oracle Human Trace |
|---|---|---|---|
| Win Rate (%) $\uparrow$ | 85.5 | 93.0 | 92.0 |
| Avg Rounds $\downarrow$ | 10.92 | 8.65 | 8.44 |
| Avg Final Score $\uparrow$ | 8.815 | 9.390 | 9.315 |

As shown in Table 3, removing the rigid structural constraints from the OP caused the Persuader’s win rates to artificially skyrocket (from 77.5% up to 93.0% for the ’Self-Routed Heuristics’ setup) and artificially shortened the debate lengths.

This finding demonstrates a critical vulnerability in standard MAD evaluations: Evaluation Collapse. Without strict internal CoT resistance mechanisms, the OP agent defaults to sycophantic agreement, yielding long before genuine persuasion has occurred. This proves that evaluating persuasion capabilities requires aggressively constraining the OP; otherwise, benchmark metrics merely capture an LLM’s inherent compliance rather than the Persuader’s true rhetorical skill.

Table 4 shows that adding a separate “Delegated Skill Router” agent, whose sole purpose is to evaluate the debate context and offload skill selection from the main Persuader, degraded performance (win rate dropping from 81.5% to 63.0% in Flash 3.0). This indicates that dispersing context and decision-making across specialized agents exacerbates context loss and handoff failures in subjective domains.

## 9 Conclusion

Evaluating foundation-model agents requires examining failure trajectories beyond final scores. In subjective multi-agent environments, agents often fail due to semantic leakage and problem drift. By implementing a hierarchical Strategy Memory and shifting to a structural logic enrichment paradigm (TS-RAG) mediated by a discrete bottleneck, we successfully prevent contextual contamination and preserve cross-domain reasoning. TS-RAG acts as a transformative capability bridge in asymmetric deployments, allowing lightweight models to consistently persuade parametrically superior opponents by isolating structural vulnerabilities. Finally, our trade-off analyses reveal that rigorous evaluation requires heavily constrained Original Poster (OP) agents; without strict resistance guardrails, they default to sycophantic compliance, which artificially inflates success metrics.

To guarantee robust cross-domain evaluation, the r/ChangeMyView structured dataset (initially featuring 100 fine-grained sub-domains) was rigorously partitioned into 9 active macro-domains, ensuring that the target evaluation domain contained minimal vocabulary overlap with the source retrieval domains.

### A.1 Experimental Splits

- 1. Testing Set (Education, Development & Family - 200 items): Utilized as the strictly held-out cross-domain testing set in this paper. Abstract 13

14

Projected increases in the intensity and frequency of droughts in the 21st century are expected to 15

cause a significant negative impact on terrestrial gross primary productivity (GPP). Yet, the 16

relative impact of soil water supply (indicated by soil moisture) and atmospheric water demand 17

(indicated by vapour pressure deficit, VPD) on GPP remains debated, primarily due to their 18

strong covariations, the presence of confounding factors, and unresolved causal relationships 19

among the interconnected hydrometeorological drivers of GPP. In this study, using a causality- 20

guided explainable artificial intelligence framework, we show that soil moisture is the dominant 21

regulator of water stress, surpassing the role of VPD, when and where soil water supply limits 22

ecosystem functions. Temporally, we use in-situ flux tower data to demonstrate that soil moisture 23

dominates the GPP response during periods of insufficient soil water supply. Spatially, we assess 24

the global spatial patterns of satellite sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (a proxy for GPP) in 25

water-limited regions and demonstrate that they are mostly dominated by soil moisture. 26

Conversely, VPD plays a greater role in controlling the temporal and spatial variations in GPP 27

than soil moisture when and where soil water supply is not limited. The relative role of soil 28

moisture and VPD is modulated by plant adaptation to long-term climatological aridity and plant 29

functional types. Our findings reconcile the ongoing debate over the impacts of soil and 30

atmospheric dryness on ecosystem functions. They provide crucial insights into how terrestrial 31

ecosystems respond to increasing aridity and more frequent droughts, particularly given the 32

potential ecosystem shifts from energy to water limitation. 33

Introduction 35

36

Terrestrial ecosystems offset approximately one-third of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO2) 37

emissions and this capacity depends on photosynthesis (indicated by the gross primary 38

productivity, GPP). However, this critical ecosystem function shows large variability across 39

space and time1, as plants often experience sub-optimal conditions with limited availability of 40

either energy (e.g. radiation and temperature) or water2,3. Water availability, determined by the 41

dynamic balance between water supply and demand, has been identified as the primary driver of 42

spatiotemporal GPP variations, particularly in dry tropical and dryland biomes4–7. On the one 43


<!-- Page 4 -->


hand, water supply from soil moisture (SM), as quantified by volumetric water content (VWC), 44

can determine the accessible water for plant growth and function2. On the other hand, the water 45

demand by the atmosphere, as quantified by vapour pressure deficit (VPD), determines the 46

diffusion of water vapour from plants to the atmosphere, and under conditions of intensified 47

atmospheric dryness, stomata on leaves tend to close to avoid excessive water loss8. The increase 48

in severity and frequency of soil droughts and atmospheric aridity events has led to reduced 49

carbon uptake and a heightened risk of plant mortality6,9–12. Additionally, under conditions of low 50

water availability, SM and VPD are highly (anti)correlated through land-atmosphere 51

coupling13,14. This coupling further exacerbates the water stress on plants, as VPD increases 52

when SM is low because of reduced evapotranspiration15. With terrestrial ecosystems 53

increasingly shifting from energy to water limitation16, it becomes imperative to understand the 54

relative influence of soil supply and atmospheric demand on plant water stress for accurately 55

predicting future land carbon uptake, especially as the rise in VPD is globally widespread yet SM 56

limitations are more localized in space and time. 57

58

Despite the growing body of literature showing the negative impacts of the trends and variations 59

of SM17–19 and VPD20,21 on plant growth and function, their relative role in driving GPP over 60

natural ecosystems remains under substantial debate19,20,22–28. Disentangling their impacts on 61

GPP is challenging for several reasons: First, SM and VPD often show strong covariations, 62

particularly under water-limited conditions20; second, there are confounding effects from other 63

hydrometeorological drivers of GPP, particularly incoming shortwave radiation (SW) and air 64

temperature (TA); third, a less acknowledged aspect is that the causal relationships among GPP 65

drivers vary significantly between energy- versus water-limited conditions13, as illustrated in 66

*Fig.1a and b. as illustrated in Fig.1a and b. Specifically, under water-limited conditions, a 67*

feedback loop exists among TA, VPD, and SM (Fig.1a)13,29. Low soil water supply limits the 68

energy partitioning towards latent heat flux, which is the most efficient surface cooling 69

mechanism, resulting in increased sensible heat fluxes and elevated near-surface TA and 70

VPD13,30,31. Conversely, when the soil water supply is sufficient and ecosystems are energy- 71

limited, SM does not strongly regulate evapotranspiration, and the SM-VPD coupling is weak 72

(Fig.1b)32. Nonetheless, VPD and TA remain closely linked under both conditions as described 73

by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation. The covarying TA further complicates the separation of 74


<!-- Page 5 -->


VPD and SM impacts on GPP, particularly because most photosynthetic processes are 75

temperature-dependent33. Previous attribution analyses that combine data from both conditions 76

may introduce bias in identifying dominant drivers, due to the absence of condition-dependent 77

causal representations. A framework capable of modelling the non-linear GPP dependencies on 78

its drivers, explicitly representing the distinct causal relationships among hydrometeorological 79

factors between water- and energy-limited conditions, and attributing feature importance in a 80

principled manner is therefore critical to reconciling the ongoing debate regarding the relative 81

influence of soil and water dryness on ecosystem functions under climate change. 82

A framework for quantifying individual VWC and VPD impacts on GPP 113

114

To characterize the causal relationships of the drivers of GPP, we use an XAI framework guided 115

by causal chain graphs to disentangle the relative role of SM and VPD in driving the temporal 116

and spatial variations in GPP. First, given the distinct causal structures between energy- and 117

water-limited conditions (Fig, 1a-b), we identify these two regimes in our datasets over both time 118

and space. Temporally, periods of water and energy limitations are distinguished based on the 119


<!-- Page 7 -->


relationship between daily evaporative fraction (EF, i.e. the ratio of latent heat to available 120

energy)39 and surface SM. As an indicator of ecosystem function, EF increases with SM when 121

ecosystems are limited by soil water supply, until reaching a critical threshold. Beyond this 122

threshold, EF tends to stabilize as soil water supply does not limit ecosystem functions, and 123

i.e. the ratio of mean annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration estimated by the 125

Second, we mapped out the complex non-linear dependency of GPP on its hydrometeorological 132

drivers using an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model across both water- and energy- 133

limited conditions in time and space. XGBoost, an advanced regression tree method, has 134

demonstrated excellent performance in identifying linear and non-linear interactions in tabular 135

Third, we used an approach called the Causal Shapley value45, which incorporates causal 143

relationships among GPP drivers based on Pearl’s causal inference do-calculus46, to interpret the 144

XGBoost models for disentangling the respective effects of VPD and SM on GPP. The Shapley 145

value, a concept developed from cooperative game theory, provides a unified and robust solution 146

for calculating the marginal contributions of model predictors (e.g. VPD and SM) to the model 147

prediction (i.e. GPP), as illustrated in Extended Data Fig.147. The absolute Shapley value for a 148

predictor represents its contribution to a specific model prediction at one data sample (i.e. local 149

contribution), while the average of all absolute Shapley values for a predictor represents its 150


<!-- Page 8 -->


overall contribution to model predictions across all data samples (i.e. global importance)48. In 151

contrast to the traditional XAI technique SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), which assumes 152

independence among predictors49, the Causal Shapley value employs causal chain graphs based 153

on expert domain knowledge to enhance the causal interpretation for machine learning models, 154

therefore effectively addressing the independence assumption inherent in SHAP (see Methods 155

for more details about the Causal Shapley value and SHAP)50,51. This approach explicitly 156

considers the different causal structures between water- and energy-limited conditions, enabling 157

a more accurate interpretation of the contributions of VPD and SM to GPP variations in the 158

context of causality. 159

Discussion 294

295

Recent studies have attempted to disentangle the effects of SM and VPD on GPP in the context 296

of warming-driven VPD increase and more frequent and intense soil droughts. However, the 297

relative importance of SM and VPD to GPP is still subject to debate. The opposing viewpoints 298

have arisen from percentile- and linearity-based analyses that cannot fully characterize the causal 299

relationships among GPP drivers or specifying data distribution under water- and energy-limited 300

conditions (Fig.1c). Using a causality-guided XAI framework, this study demonstrates that SM 301

(VPD) dominates the dryness response of GPP compared to VPD (SM) in both time and space 302

under water (energy) limitation. Long-term climatological aridity, PFTs, and hydraulic traits may 303

modulate the relative dominance of SM and VPD on the spatial pattern of GPP, leading to a more 304

nuanced response. 305

306

Incorporating causal structure into model interpretation is critical for robust quantitative analysis 307

of feature importance, particularly in the presence of confounders. Confounders are a prevalent 308

challenge when interpreting the dependency of ecological processes on their 309


<!-- Page 14 -->


hydrometeorological drivers. Traditional parametric statistics, rooted in frequentist principles and 310

linear assumptions, often struggle to unravel the complex non-linear and causal processes 311

associated with photosynthesis, unlike the techniques used in this study62. XAI techniques 312

present a promising solution for disentangling the non-linear SM and VPD effects on GPP while 313

controlling for effects of confounding factors. However, traditional XAI approaches often fail to 314

address the distinct causal relationships under water- and energy-limited conditions (Fig.1a and 315

b)13, potentially biasing the attribution analyses. To better illustrate this issue, we here compared 316

the relative importance of SM and VPD for GPP as computed from SHAP and the Causal 317

Shapley value. The analyses based on SHAP suggest a more significant role of VPD in 318

controlling GPP than SM under both water- and energy-limited conditions (Supplementary 319

*Fig.5), which contrasts with previous findings that SM dominates the variations in GPP under 320*

arid conditions19,25,26,63,64. Additionally, two SHAP-based studies examining the influence of SM 321

and VPD on GPP at flux sites yield contradictory findings on their relative importance, likely due 322

to strong covariations among the model predictors43,44. 323

324

Delineating the water- and energy-limited conditions in the analysis is critical for interpreting the 325

relative role of SM and VPD in controlling GPP. Indeed, the impact of SM on GPP tends to 326

diminish under energy-limited conditions when and where water supply is sufficient, while VPD 327

has a persistent negative impact on GPP under both water- and energy-limited conditions due to 328

its direct regulation of stomatal conductance (Extended Data Fig.4 and 5). Ecosystem functions 329

usually show the highest sensitivity to SM and VPD during periods of severe dryness17,27. Under 330

such extreme conditions, SM has a significantly stronger impact on GPP than VPD in grasslands, 331

savannahs, shrublands, and at the global scale, while their contributions are similar in the forest 332

flux sites (Welch’s t-tests, P < 0.05) (Extended Data Fig.6). By analyzing the SM data in the 333

forest flux sites, we found that two sandy forest sites, a deciduous broadleaf forest (DBF, ZM- 334

Mon) and an evergreen needleleaf forest (ENF, NL-Loo), primarily contributed to the diminished 335

negative impact of SM on GPP (indicated by the dashed box in Extended Data Fig.2d). These 336

forests exhibit high resilience to low SM (typically below 10%), likely because they have 337

adapted to well-drained conditions and developed extensive root systems to access deep water 338

sources (see FLUXNET2015 site descriptions). When conditions become energy-limited, the 339

impact of SM on GPP diminishes, making VPD the limiting water availability factor (Extended 340


<!-- Page 15 -->


Data Fig.3). Indeed, previous studies also find that SM plays a larger role than VPD  in dryland 341

ecosystems19,26,63 and during drought/heatwave events25,64, while VPD is more dominant than 342

SM when considering data from all periods20,24,43 or on a global scale23,65 as ecosystems are 343

typically unstressed in terms of water supply. 344

345

Both dry and humid biomes have developed a broad range of strategies, including physiological, 346

biochemical, morphological, and anatomical adaptations, to cope with conditions of water or 347

energy limitations61,66–68. For example, in water-limited regions, dryland biomes show high 348

diversity of rooting depths, with shallow and deep roots coexisting within the biomes, enabling 349

efficient use of available surface water from rainfall or access to deeper stored water61. Non- 350

woody biomes (e.g. SAV, WSA, SH, and GRA), growing under larger deficits of annual 351

precipitation relative to potential evapotranspiration, show a higher dependence on SM 352

(Extended Data Fig.5a), indicating an adaptation to long-term climatological aridity. 353

Characterized by shallow rooting depths (Supplementary Fig.5a), non-woody biomes tend to be 354

more dependent on precipitation as the primary source of soil water supply. Conversely, most dry 355

woody biomes with greater rooting depth are more sensitive to atmospheric evaporative demand 356

than soil drought (Fig.3c; Supplementary Fig.6a), likely due to their access to deep water 357

reservoirs. In addition to morphological traits, hydrological traits can also modulate the 358

sensitivity of ecosystem functions to SM and VPD. More isohydric plants tend to actively 359

regulate stomatal conductance to keep a steady leaf water potential during droughts, albeit at the 360

cost of reduced carbon uptake. Conversely, more anisohydric plants tend to maintain high rates 361

of photosynthesis and transpiration to potentially outperform their isohydric competitors during 362

droughts, despite the increased risk of xylem embolism59. More anisohydric GRA and OSH 363

appear to be more sensitive to VPD than SM compared to their more isohydric counterparts 364

(Extended Data Fig.5d), indicating that high atmospheric evaporative demand can have larger 365

negative impacts on ecosystems with less strict regulation of stomatal closure, which is 366

consistent with previous findings69. 367

368

In humid areas, VPD emerges as the most widespread limiting factor of water availability 369

(Fig.3b). A limited proportion of these areas are identified as SM-dominated, including ENF in 370

south Canada and evergreen broadleaf forests (EBF) in parts of the Amazon and Congo basins 371


<!-- Page 16 -->


(Fig.3b). These areas align well with the spatial patterns of ecosystems that demonstrate a 372

relative decoupling between their functions and drought impacts in ref54 (Supplementary Fig.2g). 373

However, accumulating evidence suggests that more severe droughts induced by climate change 374

can lead to significant reductions in productivity and increased tree mortality once water scarcity 375

exceeds their hydraulic safety thresholds10,11,70. The high reliance of the productivity of these 376

ecosystems on SM highlights the importance of soil water supply in safeguarding their critical 377

ecosystem services under future climate change. South Canada and the Amazon basin have also 378

been identified as hot spots of a fast transition from energy to water limitation16. Additionally, 379

using a space-for-time analogy, our findings on spatial variability of annual SIF is consistent with 380

previous studies that indicate SM dominates the interannual variability of carbon uptake in 381

tropical forests71,72. Canopy height has been shown to be a regulator for the sensitivity of plant 382

functions to VPD. Plants require efficient long-distance water transport through xylems to lift 383

soil water from the roots to the leaves for transpiration73. Taller plants may exhibit increased 384

stomatal sensitivity to VPD due to augmented gravitational and friction head losses8. This pattern 385

is observed in ENF and WSA (Extended Data Fig.6f). In tall forests with dense canopies, the 386

high water uptake needs can lead to competition for soil water, positioning SM as a limiting 387

factor73. 388

389

The choice of SM measurements from different soil depths may somewhat influence our result. 390

For example, comparing the influence of surface SM and VPD on eddy covariance GPP in 391

forests revealed a more substantial role of VPD on GPP than SM (Supplementary Fig.3a). Yet, 392

trees may have access to deeper root zone moisture compared to surface soil moisture so that the 393

results based on surface SM might overestimate the occurrence of soil water stress. Indeed, plant 394

functions are closely correlated with surface SM in areas with low tree cover, while regions with 395

dense forests are more responsive to changes in deeper water storage56. Under water-limited 396

conditions, forests show increased vulnerability to deficits in deep soil water compared to surface 397

water27,74. Furthermore, the sensitivity of GPP to SM at different soil depths can be dynamically 398

modulated by the position of the water table relative to the rooting depth; however, we still lack 399

such observational root zone SM data at most eddy-covariance sites. Another uncertainty is that 400

TA, VPD and SM are treated equivalently with bidirected edges under water-limited conditions 401

(Fig.1a). According to the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, TA is the cause of VPD through its direct 402


<!-- Page 17 -->


effect on saturation vapour pressure. Causal chain graphs have limited capacities to represent 403

more complex causal structures. However, we argue that this limitation might lead to an 404

overestimation of the importance of VPD, which does not alter the finding that SM plays a more 405

dominant role than VPD in driving GPP under water-limited conditions. 406

407

Conclusions 408

409

In this study, we developed a causality-guided explainable AI framework to reconcile the 410

ongoing debate about the relative role of soil water supply and atmospheric evaporative demand 411

in controlling ecosystem functions. We used long-term eddy covariance GPP data and 412

TROPOMI SIF as a proxy of ecosystem photosynthesis, and classified water- and energy-limited 413

conditions based on soil moisture thresholds in time and wetness index thresholds in space. Our 414

framework quantified the relative contributions of soil moisture and VPD on GPP by 415

disentangling their individual effects from confounding factors and explicitly incorporating 416

causal relationships under water and energy limitations. Our global analyses provide a conclusive 417

answer to the question of ecosystem responses to water stress: soil moisture predominantly 418

controls GPP variations when and where soil water supply limits ecosystem functions. When and 419

where soil water supply is no longer limiting, photosynthesis becomes more responsive to VPD 420

rather than soil moisture. Long-term climatic aridity, plant functional types and ecosystem-scale 421

hydraulic traits can further modulate the relative role of soil moisture and VPD in controlling 422

GPP. Specifically, dryland biomes with lower deficits of precipitation relative to potential 423

evapotranspiration, and humid biomes that have larger rooting depths and/or lower resistance to 424

drought, tend to show greater dependence on VPD than SM, respectively. 425

426

As a consequence of anthropogenic climate change and land-atmosphere interactions, the 427

frequency and intensity of atmospheric aridity and soil droughts are projected to continue 428

increasing in the future. With terrestrial ecosystems shifting towards water limitation and 429

increasing extreme drought and heatwave events12,16, soil moisture is expected to be an 430

increasingly limiting factor for ecosystem functions, especially for water-limited periods and 431

regions. Furthermore, with rising temperatures and decreasing relative humidity8,21, VPD is 432

expected to increase dramatically across the globe. Both factors should induce further stress on 433


<!-- Page 18 -->


water and energy-limited conditions and impact global GPP. Plants may acclimate and adapt to 434

those changes but the extent to which they can remains a significant source of uncertainty8,75. 435

This interplay between stress and acclimation or adaptation is likely going to have a major 436

impact on future photosynthesis and the capacity of ecosystems to continue to act as a major 437

carbon sink. 438

Methods 440

441

FLUXNET2015 data 442

443

We selected natural eddy covariance sites from the global FLUXNET2015 database35 that had 444

observation lengths longer than five years. We grouped flux sites into three primary categories 445

following ref43, namely forests, grasslands, as well as savannahs-shrublands. Evergreen broadleaf 446

forests (EBF), deciduous broadleaf forests (DBF), evergreen needleleaf forests (ENF), and mixed 447

forests (MF) were classified as forests. Closed and open shrublands (CSH and OSH), woody 448

savannas (WSA), and savannas (SAV) were classified as savannahs and shrublands. The 449

predictors included SW, TA, VPD, soil surface volumetric water content (VWC, %) for 450

grasslands, savannahs and shrublands, and soil top 1–3 layer VWC for forests. Ultimately, 44 451

sites were chosen, including nine PFTs as classified by the International Geosphere–Biosphere 452

Programme (IGBP) (Table S1). We selected these sites mainly according to data availability for 453

SM data of the top three layers for forests and the surface layer for drylands and grasslands. We 454

excluded croplands in the analyses due to the influence of anthropogenic water management. 455

456

Growing-season half-hourly GPP data estimated by the nighttime partitioning method 457

(GPP_NT_VUT_REF) were used as the dependence variable76. We did not use the GPP data 458

estimated by the daytime partitioning because the algorithm incorporated an empirical function 459

of the VPD effect on GPP77. Site-specific growing seasons were determined by the periods when 460

daily GPP exceeded the 30% percentile of GPP observations for each year and when TA was 461

above 0 °C. Moreover, we chose the data with GPP > 0 µmol m-2 s-1, SW > 50 W m-2, and 462

VPD > 5 hPa for further analyses. We incorporated four predominant hydrometeorological 463

factors of GPP, including SW (W m-2), TA (°C), VPD (hPa), and VWC (%), when training the 464


<!-- Page 19 -->


XGBoost models for estimating GPP. Other factors, such as ambient CO2 concentrations and 465

wind speed, were not used considering their less predictive role in half-hourly GPP43. The data 466

were filtered based on the quality flags (_QC suffix variables) provided by the FLUXNET2015 467

database (NEE_VUT_REF_QC for GPP). 468

469

Categorizing water and energy limitations in flux data 470

471

Following refs2,3, we analyzed the relationship between daily surface-layer VWC and the 472

evaporative fraction (EF) during dry-downs to identify water- and energy-limited periods for 473

each site. EF increases with SM when the ecosystem is water-limited and becomes saturated 474

once SM exceeds a critical threshold, beyond which the ecosystem is considered energy- 475

limited16. EF is calculated as the ratio of latent heat fluxes (LE) to the sum of sensible heat fluxes 476

(H) and LE. Dry-downs refer to the intervals during the growing season when surface-layer SM 477

continuously decreases for at least n consecutive days following a rainfall event. n was set to 10 478

in ref2, while we adjusted it between 3 and 14 days to obtain the best fit for each site. However, 479

we still did not observe a water-energy limitation transition for some sites (Supplementary Table 480

1), and we used the SM thresholds derived from the EF-SM relationships based on the sites with 481

observation lengths longer than 10 years under three categories for these sites (Extended Data 482

*Fig.7). The identified SM thresholds are within the range of those reported in ref2. The 483*

transitional point of SM was identified using a linear-plateau model with the R package 484

'minpack.lm'. 485

486

Global products 487

488

We derived global annually-averaged gridded TROPOMI far-red SIF (740 nm) at a 0.083° 489

resolution for 2020 (Supplementary Fig.1a), using quality-controlled data aggregated from 8-day 490

intervals38. The TROPOMI spectrometer on the Sentinel-5 Precursor, launched in October 2017, 491

outperforms earlier satellite products by offering fine spatial and temporal resolutions of global 492

SIF observations38. Low-quality SIF data affected by high cloud fractions and large viewing 493

zenith angles were excluded38. 494

495


<!-- Page 20 -->


Global climatic data were obtained from reanalysis products for 2020. The annual average 2-m 496

TA, surface solar radiation downwards, 2-m dew-point temperature, and SM for layers 1 and 2 497

(0–7 and 7–28 cm depths) were derived from monthly ERA5-Land reanalysis data in ~9 km 498

resolution78. We calculated 2-m VPD based on 2-m monthly TA and dew-point temperature 499

according to the Clausius-Clapeyron relation. The land cover information for 2020 was derived 500

from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) MCD12C1 product (version 501

6), which provides IGBP maps in 0.05° resolution79. Additionally, we explored the potential 502

factors that modulate the relative role of SM and VPD in controlling GPP. The spatial patterns of 503

ecosystem-scale hydraulic traits, including apparent rooting depths (Zr)57, the xylem water 504

potential measured at 50 % xylem conductivity loss (Ψ50)58, and the degree of anisohydricity59, 505

were derived from their global datasets. We obtained a global 10-m resolution map of canopy 506

height for 2020, which was built by fusing space-borne LiDAR data and satellite optical images 507

using a deep learning model60. 508

509

We used the wetness index (WI) derived from the TerraClimate climatology product (~4 km) to 510

categorize the grid cells into water- and energy-limited areas. WI is calculated as the ratio of 511

long-term annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration80. Larger WI values indicate wetter 512

and lower WI values indicate drier. All global products were resampled to 0.05° and trimmed for 513

the area between 60° north and south latitudes for further analyses. 514

515

Mapping GPP dependencies on its drivers using XGBoost 516

517

Tree-based models typically outperform other machine learning algorithms when tackling 518

regression of tabular data41. Here we mapped the predominant abiotic drivers into eddy 519

covariance GPP and TROPOMI SIF using a tree-based XGBoost algorithm81. XGBoost excels in 520

efficiently handling tabular datasets and outperforms other tree-based models by leveraging 521

advanced regularization and parallel computing techniques82. It iteratively constructs a series of 522

trees, each one aimed at correcting the residuals of its predecessor, and continues this cycle until 523

a predefined root mean square error (RMSE) is achieved. A distinctive feature of XGBoost is its 524

capability to handle both linear and non-linear relationships, making it suited for modeling 525

complex relationships between GPP/SIF and their drivers. Predictors include SW, TA, VPD, SM, 526


<!-- Page 21 -->


and a category variable (Site_ID) for training eddy covariance GPP models, where Site_ID is 527

used to remove the spatial information contained in flux data. Site_ID is omitted in TROPOMI 528

SIF models. The hyperparameters of XGBoost models were fine-tuned through five-fold cross- 529

validation grid search. We used 80% of the dataset for training and retained 20% for testing. To 530

minimize the uncertainty caused by random splitting, we trained three models for each category 531

of flux sites and for both dryland and non-dryland over the space. The trained models perform 532

reasonably well in explaining the spatiotemporal variations in eddy covariance GPP and 533

TROPOMI SIF, with coefficients of determination (R2) ranging between 0.63 and 0.86 534

(Supplementary Table S2). 535

## Abstract

Wide-field searches for young stellar objects (YSOs) can place useful constraints on the prevalence of clustered versus distributed star formation. The Spitzer/IRAC Candidate YSO (SPICY) catalog is one of the largest compilations of such objects ( $\sim$ 120,000 candidates in the Galactic midplane). Many SPICY candidates are spatially clustered, but, perhaps surprisingly, approximately half the candidates appear spatially distributed. To better characterize this unexpected population and confirm its nature, we obtained Palomar/DBSP spectroscopy for 26 of the optically-bright ( $G<15$ mag) “isolated” YSO candidates. We confirm the YSO classifications of all 26 sources based on their positions on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, H and Ca ii line-emission from over half the sample, and robust detection of infrared excesses. This implies a contamination rate of $<$ 10% for SPICY stars that meet our optical selection criteria. Spectral types range from B4 to K3, with A-type stars most common. Spectral energy distributions, diffuse interstellar bands, and Galactic extinction maps indicate moderate to high extinction. Stellar masses range from $\sim$ 1–7 $M_{\odot}$ , and the estimated accretion rates, ranging from $3\times 10^{-8}$ to $3\times 10^{-7}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr-1, are typical for YSOs in this mass range. The 3D spatial distribution of these stars, based on Gaia astrometry, reveals that the “isolated” YSOs are not evenly distributed in the Solar neighborhood but are concentrated in kpc-scale dusty Galactic structures that also contain the majority of the SPICY YSO clusters. Thus, the processes that produce large Galactic star-forming structures may yield nearly as many distributed as clustered YSOs.

#### Keywords:

## I Introduction

Young stellar objects (YSOs) exhibit a high degree of spatial clustering [24, 84, 81, 99], which arises as a consequence of the hierarchical structure of the molecular clouds from which they form [98, 76, 52]. Most known YSOs are found in star-forming complexes that may contain hundreds to thousands of stars [112, 113]. Theoretical models of star formation on a Galactic scale tend to focus on massive star-forming regions, which are thought to domination the star-formation rate [88, 75, e.g.,].

Nevertheless, there are many examples of YSOs that appear to be in relative isolation or small groups. These range from the nearest YSOs in the TW Hya Association [150], to small clusters around Herbig Ae/Be stars [60], molecular clouds with low stellar yields [109, 42], and O stars that appear to be located outside major star-forming regions [104].

The prevalence of clustered versus distributed star formation has implications for star-formation theory. For example, supersonic turbulence in molecular clouds, proposed as a possible regulatory mechanism for the star-formation rate of the Galaxy [74], is expected to influence the spatial distribution of young stars. Strong turbulent pressure support would produce isolated star-forming cores, while dense clusters could form more easily in its absence [91].

Astronomical surveys that provide coverage over large areas of the sky can be useful when searching for distributed YSOs outside known star-forming regions. However, in these searches, contamination rates are expected to be higher for isolated YSO candidates than for clustered YSO candidates, given that contaminants tend to be uniformly distributed [93, 79, e.g.,].

The Spitzer/IRAC Candidate YSO (SPICY) catalog [77, hereafter Paper I] is one of the most extensive censuses of YSOs in the Galactic midplane, the region of the Galaxy with the highest star-formation activity. This catalog contains $\sim$ 105 candidate YSOs, selected by their mid-infrared properties from the Galactic Legacy Infrared Mid-Plane Survey Extraordinaire [10, 30, GLIMPSE;], and related projects.

As expected, the SPICY YSOs trace out numerous young star clusters, including both previously known and newly identified star-forming regions [82, hereafter Paper II]. More surprisingly, nearly 50% of the candidate YSOs do not appear spatially associated with other young stars. If this ratio of clustered-to-distributed YSOs holds, it would imply that distributed star formation contributes significantly to the Galaxy’s star-formation rate. Other survey-based censuses have also reported significant numbers of non-clustered young stellar candidates [119, 95, 96, 147, 136, 145, 97, e.g.,]. In these studies, candidate identification is typically based on photometric data and, more recently, on astrometric data from the Gaia mission [44]. Thus, follow-up observations are necessary for confirmation of YSOs. Here, we spectroscopically examine a sample of 26 YSO candidates from SPICY to test whether there is evidence for an isolated population in the Galaxy.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II summarizes the SPICY catalog and describes our criteria for selecting program stars. Section III describes observations and data reduction. Section IV provides inferred stellar properties, including spectral types, emission lines, extinctions, luminosities, masses, ages, and accretion rates. Section V presents our arguments that the program stars are all YSOs and uses this sample to constrain SPICY contamination rates. Section VI examines the Galactic environments of the program stars. Finally, Section VII provides our discussion and conclusions.

## II The SPICY Catalog

The SPICY catalog [77] contains 117,446 candidate YSOs identified using mid-infrared photometry from Spitzer/IRAC observations of the Galactic midplane, including the Galactic Legacy Infrared Mid-Plane Survey Extraordinaire (GLIMPSE) I, II, 3D, Galactic Center, Vela-Carina, Cygnus X, and Spitzer Mapping of the Outer Galaxy surveys [10, 128, 30, 92, 148, 9, 144, 145]. These were analyzed in tandem with the near-infrared photometry from the Two-Micron All Sky Survey [124, 2MASS;], the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope (UKIRT) Infrared Deep Sky Survey [87, 89, UKIDSS;], and the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy (VISTA) Variables in the Vía Láctea [102, 126, VVV;]. Altogether, the SPICY YSO catalog covers 613 square degrees near the Galactic midplane between Galactic coordinates $-105^{\circ}\leq\ell\leq 110^{\circ}$ and $|b|\lesssim 1$ –2∘.

Candidate YSOs were identified based on excess infrared emission consistent with the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of pre-main-sequence stars with disks or envelopes, using the YSOs analyzed by Povich et al. [108] as templates. A random-forest classifier was employed [61, 13], and only the near- and mid-infrared photometry, without consideration of sky coordinates, were used as features. Thus, the catalog provides a view of the distribution of YSOs in the Galactic midplane that is nearly spatially unbiased, apart from issues of Spitzer survey sensitivity in regions with differing levels of point-source crowding and mid-infrared nebulosity [69]. Infrared observations of star-forming regions tend to unveil deeply embedded YSOs that are not optically visible. In the case of SPICY, only about one third of the stars are detected by Gaia.

### II.1 Clustered and Distributed Stars in SPICY

The candidate YSOs in the SPICY catalog include both clustered and distributed stars. 77 performed cluster analysis on the Galactic $(\ell,b)$ coordinates of this sample, finding over 400 groups containing at least 30 stars via the HDBSCAN algorithm [18] using the ‘‘Excess of Mass’’ method.11 1 This initial cluster analysis was based only on angular positions in, since Gaia astrometry is unavailable for two thirds of the SPICY sample. These groups include both stellar clusters and stellar associations, and their members collectively account for half the YSO candidates [77, their Section 7]. In 82, Gaia reveals that optically visible members of the same SPICY groups tend to have similar parallaxes and proper motions, providing corroboration that they are physically associated young stars. However, this strategy cannot be used to verify the spatially distributed stars in the SPICY catalog, so other methods must be used to confirm their youth.

Here, we base our samples of “clustered” and “isolated” SPICY stars on whether the sources are included in the groups from 77. This division is algorithm dependent, since different cluster analysis algorithms may yield different results [35]. Nevertheless, the HDBSCAN algorithm has become a popular method for identifying young stellar clusters and associations [19, 72, 67, e.g.,]. It is also possible that some “isolated” SPICY stars may be members of stellar groups not detected in Paper I, which could include clusters with low disk fractions or whose members are mostly too faint to be detected. These possibilities are investigated in Section VI.
